findings.text: Exposes helpers to install a descriptor into an indexed global table slot and to build task-state and local-table system descriptors from an address plus size and kind, with per-CPU installation support for the task register entry and a macro selecting the conventional task slot.

Provides local-table installation distinguished by entry count, plus loads for global and interrupt table registers and stores for interrupt register and task register, with invalidation helpers that load an empty null-based zero-sized register image.

Supplies task-register loading including a variant that temporarily swaps a read-only mapping for a writable one, plus bulk refresh of thread-local slots from thread state and a no-op early fault-table setup hook.

The width copied into a global slot depends on the requested kind, using a wider task-state footprint for task descriptors, a wider local-table footprint for local descriptors, and a generic slot footprint otherwise.

Built system descriptors start cleared, carry the caller supplied extent and location split across low and high portions, record the supplied kind, and are marked present, with an extra high location word on wider builds.
An empty local-table request clears the hardware selector, while a populated request installs a sized present local descriptor into the conventional local slot and then loads that selector.
The native global-table load, interrupt-table load, interrupt-table store, task-register load and task-register store act as direct privileged entry points for descriptor hardware state.
The generic descriptor is a packed small record holding extent and location fragments together with access mode, privilege, presence and availability controls plus mode and granularity selectors.

The system descriptor is a packed record with extent and location fragments, kind and privilege and presence controls, and granularity plus high location handling, reused under two type aliases for task and local purposes with an additional high word on wider builds.

Interrupt handling uses a bit-field attribute bundle plus a staging record of vector, segment, attributes and handler address, a packed gate record combining offsets with segment and attributes and optional high offset, and a packed limit-plus-address image for table registers.
Gate kinds are interrupt 0xE, trap 0xF, call 0xC and task 0x5; system kinds are task-state 0x9 and local-table 0x2 with non-system marked 0x10.

Low attribute bits place accessed at 0x1, writable and readable share 0x2, expand-down and conforming share 0x4, executable at 0x8, system marker at 0x10, privilege shifted by five, present at 0x80, long mode at 0x2000, operand size at 0x4000 and page granularity at 0x8000.

Data and code templates combine system, present, accessed and writable or readable-plus-executable attributes, refined into sixteen-bit, thirty-two-bit, BIOS thirty-two-bit and sixty-four-bit variants using granularity, operand-size and long-mode controls, with a separate thirty-two-bit task-state present system value and a user privilege adjustment.

Access-right encodings place read-only data, read-write data, expand-down variants and execute-only or execute-read code with conforming variants at multiples of bit nine, privilege zero and three at multiples of bit thirteen with masks, and accessed, system, present, available, long, operand-size and granularity markers at bits eight, twelve, fifteen, twenty, twenty-one, twenty-two and twenty-three.
Early boot interrupt table holds thirty-two entries.

Two predicates distinguish an architecturally empty selector description from an all-zero description by differing expectations for access mode and presence attributes while sharing zero expectations for base, bound and remaining controls; clearing is expressed as installing a null base with zero count.

Staging validates that the vector fits in a byte, clears the staging record, records the vector and handler plus the kernel code segment, and selects an interrupt gate marked present; gate construction then distributes the handler address across low, middle and where present high portions while copying segment and attributes.

Base and limit setters distribute a scalar across the corresponding low and high fragments of a generic slot, while gate readers reassemble the handler address from its fragments and expose the stored segment.
A static initializer builds a generic slot image from flag, base and limit scalars by distributing each scalar across the corresponding bit-fields.
Local-table installation is exposed through a paravirtual dispatch taking a base and count, and the raw processor number is obtained from per-CPU storage.

Provides in-place sixty-four by thirty-two division with remainder, a sixty-four-bit dividend helper returning quotient with remainder out-parameter, thirty-two by thirty-two multiply and sixty-four plus thirty-two addition, and a combined multiply-add-divide primitive with a multiply-divide specialization.

The in-place division macro updates its dividend to the quotient and yields the remainder, using a masking and shifting fast path when the divisor is a compile-time power of two and a high-word reduction plus hardware division otherwise; the out-parameter variant zeroes the high word after extracting a possible high quotient.

Callers must ensure a non-zero divisor and a quotient that fits the expected width, since the helpers provide no visible zero or overflow checks and the combined primitive chains multiply, conditional add and divide without intermediate checks.

Legacy direct memory access is limited to eight channels, sixteen megabytes for classic transfers and four gigabytes for thirty-two-bit transfers, with the classic ceiling expressed as a page-offset plus sixteen-megabyte address on one build and as a direct-mapped translation of the classic page-frame count on the other.
Controller bases are zero and 0xC0; read mode is 0x44, write mode is 0x48, cascade is 0xC0 and auto-initialize is 0x10.

First-controller controls place command with status at 0x08, request at 0x09, single mask at 0x0A, mode at 0x0B, flip-flop clear at 0x0C, temporary with reset at 0x0D, clear mask at 0x0E and full mask at 0x0F.

Second-controller controls place command with status at 0xD0, request at 0xD2, single mask at 0xD4, mode at 0xD6, flip-flop clear at 0xD8, temporary with reset at 0xDA, clear mask at 0xDC and full mask at 0xDE.

Per-channel address ports are 0x00, 0x02, 0x04, 0x06 for low channels and 0xC0, 0xC4, 0xC8, 0xCC for high channels; count ports are 0x01, 0x03, 0x05, 0x07 and 0xC2, 0xC6, 0xCA, 0xCE; page ports are 0x87, 0x83, 0x81, 0x82 and 0x8B, 0x89, 0x8A with no page entry for channel four.

Direct memory access programming is serialized by a spin lock with interrupt state saved and restored across the critical section through paired claim and release helpers returning and accepting flags.

Channel control selects the first or second controller by channel number, masking and mode selection combine the channel index with the requested code, address installation programs a page byte then low and high bytes with halved addressing on upper channels, count installation stores one less than requested with similar halving, and residue reading reassembles low and high bytes with doubling on upper channels.

Page programming has no entry for the cascade channel and masks the low bit on upper channels, output width selection depends on build configuration, and residue relies on sixteen-bit wrap with an added one.
Direct-memory-access byte output selects a pausing variant on one build and a plain variant on the other, while byte input is a direct alias.

Exposes the architecture direct-memory-access operation table, an early boot allocator for firmware table handling, early and normal firmware mapping aliases, a no-op double-fault task setup, and include guards for descriptor, division, mapping, direct-memory, firmware, fault, unwind and memory-map headers.
Unwind support maps canonical frame directive names to the underlying assembler directives for procedure boundaries, address computation, offset adjustments and state handling.

A per-CPU invalid marker tracks whether the task-state limit needs reloading: refresh reloads only when marked invalid, invalidation reloads immediately when an input-output bitmap is present and otherwise only marks invalid, and successful reload clears the marker.
Reload ensures the task entry is in an available rather than busy condition for the privileged load to succeed, finishing with the entry loaded and the invalid marker cleared.

Task-limit maintenance warns when callable with preemption enabled and depends on stable per-CPU state and thread flags, while task-register loading on one variant depends on the current table base matching the expected read-only mapping before swapping.
